learning_outcomes.text: Apply acquired knowledge to elaborate and defend arguments that allow them to transmit information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Solve problems with initiative, make informed decisions, and be autonomous and creative.
Engage in critical and logical reasoning.

Have a deep knowledge of the fundamental principles and models of computation and know how to apply them to interpret, select, value, model, and create new concepts, theories, uses, and technological developments.
Handle, fluently, the languages of Propositional Logic and Predicate Logic.
Prove the validity of a simple formula in both logics using different procedures.
Translate simple sentences from natural language to the most appropriate Logic language.
Check the correctness of a simple reasoning.
Understand the concept of an axiomatic system and its relationship with the semantics of Logic.
Transform a sentence into its clausal form.
Know and manage the proof procedure using general resolution.
Understand the concept of an algorithm and differentiate what is and what is not algorithmic.
Know a model of computation as a framework for constructing codes of computable functions.
Know how to adequately use the fundamental results of Computability: Universality, Parametrization, and Recursion.
Understand the concept of unsolvability and know techniques for studying problem solvability to differentiate what is computable from what is not.

syllabus_topics: Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms and Propositional Resolution
Clausal Form, Unification, and General Resolution
Theme 3. Models of Computation and Computable Functions
Theme 4. Fundamental Results and Problem Solvability
Fundamental theorems: Universality, Parametrization and Recursion
assessment_rules: For the ordinary assessment, students must obtain a minimum of 5 out of 10 points in both Partial Exam 1 (P1) and Partial Exam 2 (P2). If these minimums are met, the final grade is calculated as (0.45 x P1) + (0.45 x P2) + (0.10 x PA). If the minimums are not met, the final grade will be the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. For extraordinary assessments, a single theoretical exam covers both parts (P1 and P2), each requiring a minimum of 5 points out of 10. The final grade is (0.5 x P1) + (0.5 x P2); otherwise, it is the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. In case of doubt regarding authorship or unauthorized means (e.g., AI tools), students may be asked to defend their work in person.
